1128.title: Nataraja explained
1128.hook: one arm swings across the body like an elephant's trunk, and the hand at the end of it doesn't grab: it points at a lifted foot
1128.howItsDone: Tamil hymns to Nataraja praise the lifted foot, which the lower hand points to; in worship, flowers are laid at the god's feet, and touching the feet of elders and teachers is a sign of respect.

segments.voice: Yesterday in Nataraja explained, the flame: the ending, held level with the drum's beginning. Today, the lower hands, and where one of them points.
screen: `THE BEGINNING IN ONE HAND, THE ENDING IN THE OTHER.` · `TODAY: WHERE THE HAND POINTS.`

segments.voice: A guide at a busy train station doesn't take your suitcase or drag you to the platform. She lifts an arm and points: that way, platform four. Then she lets you walk. Nataraja has a hand like that. Of his two lower hands, one is raised palm out, the do-not-fear gesture from the mudras. The other is the one to watch today. It swings across his chest and hangs loose, and the fingers point down and across the body, at his raised foot.
screen: `A GUIDE WHO POINTS: THAT WAY.` → `ONE LOWER HAND: DO NOT FEAR.` → `THE OTHER POINTS AT THE FOOT.`

segments.voice: That arm has a name in the language of dance: gaja hasta, the elephant hand, because it hangs across the body the way an elephant's trunk swings. In a family where the son has an elephant's head, it's a gentle touch. Notice what the hand doesn't do. It doesn't hold anything, or grab, or push. It points, at the lifted foot. One foot is planted, pressing down; what's under it comes tomorrow. The other leg swings across, the foot lifted clear of the ground. In the usual reading, the planted foot presses down and holds, and the lifted foot is release: the way out, the grace that lifts you clear. So the image is giving directions. Here is the way out, says the hand. Look there. That fits the place feet have in Hindu devotion. Children may touch the feet of their parents and teachers. In temples, flowers are laid at the god's feet. In devotional poetry, taking refuge at the feet of the divine is a way of saying surrender, trust, coming home. The Tamil poet-saint Appar sang about this very foot. In paraphrase: if you could see the arched brow, the smile on the lips, the matted hair and the lifted golden foot of the dancer, then being born a human on this earth would be worth it. Not a ticket out of the world. A reason to be glad you're in it. The hand doesn't drag you there. It points, and leaves the walking to you.
screen: `GAJA HASTA, THE ELEPHANT HAND.` · `IT DOESN'T GRAB. IT POINTS.` · `THE LIFTED FOOT: RELEASE.` · `APPAR: WORTH BEING BORN FOR.` · then, large: `IT POINTS, AND LEAVES THE WALKING TO YOU.`

segments.voice: Let your left arm rest loosely across your lap, fingers soft and pointing down, and follow its line down to your feet on the floor. Notice which foot feels heavier, more planted, then let the other feel a little lighter, as if it could lift, and breathe there, between the planted and the light. If you pray, you can bring your thoughts to the feet of Shiva, or to God, in your own words.
Nataraja explained. Today, the gaja hasta, the elephant hand that swings across the body and points to the lifted foot: release, and the way out.
Your line: Nataraja explained. Appar thought one glimpse of that lifted foot made a human birth worth having. Back tomorrow, same hill.

1129.title: Nataraja explained
1129.hook: under the planted foot lies a small figure on his belly, and the dancer never finishes him off
1129.howItsDone: In Nataraja images the right foot rests on Apasmara, a small figure read as ignorance or forgetfulness; the story of the forest sages, the tiger, the snake and the dwarf is told in the temple tradition of Chidambaram.

segments.voice: Yesterday in Nataraja explained, the elephant hand pointed to the lifted foot. Today, the other foot, and who's under it.
screen: `IT POINTS, AND LEAVES THE WALKING TO YOU.` · `TODAY: UNDER THE FOOT.`

segments.voice: He's the easiest part of the image to miss. Look down past the swinging arms and the flying hair to Nataraja's right foot, the planted one. Under it, flat on his belly, lies a small, round-limbed figure, often holding a snake, pinned to the ground. He isn't the hero of anything. He's closer to the name that was right there a second ago, or the reason you walked into this room: gone. Small, daily, and always back. His name is Apasmara.
screen: `EASY TO MISS.` → `UNDER THE PLANTED FOOT.` → `HIS NAME: APASMARA.`

segments.voice: In the usual reading, Apasmara is ignorance, the forgetfulness that hides what's true, the mind losing hold of itself. There's a story behind him, told in the temple tradition of Chidambaram and retold by the art historian Ananda Coomaraswamy. In a forest lived a community of sages, proud of their own rites, who thought they had no need of Shiva. He came among them in disguise, and they were furious, so they used their powers against him. First they sent a tiger. Shiva caught it, peeled off its skin, and wore it at his waist. Then a snake: he hung it around his neck like a garland. Then a dwarf, a malicious little creature. Shiva put his foot on its back and began to dance, and the sages, watching, gave up their pride. Here's the detail worth keeping. Shiva never kills Apasmara. He doesn't kick him off the stage or crush him. He keeps him under the foot, and keeps dancing. Some readers say that's honest about forgetting: it doesn't go away for good, not in this life, and has to be kept down, gently, again and again. Some go further: if forgetfulness were destroyed outright, nobody would have to make the effort of remembering, and the effort is part of the path. Either way, the dancer isn't anxious about it. The calm face sits right above the foot that holds forgetting down. Remembering isn't a victory you win once. It's a step you keep taking.
screen: `APASMARA: FORGETTING, IGNORANCE.` · `TIGER, SNAKE, DWARF FROM THE SAGES.` · `HE IS HELD DOWN, NEVER KILLED.` · `THE EFFORT IS PART OF THE PATH.` · then, large: `REMEMBERING IS A STEP YOU KEEP TAKING.`

segments.voice: With both feet flat on the floor, rest your attention in the right foot: the heel, the ball, the toes. When the mind wanders off into a plan or a memory, that's Apasmara, and it's fine: press the right foot gently into the floor, just enough to feel it, and let the attention settle back. If you pray, you can say Shiva's name, or the name of God you use, each time you come back.
Nataraja explained. Today, Apasmara under the planted foot: forgetting, held down and never killed, so that remembering stays a step the dancer keeps taking.
Your line: Nataraja explained. Forgetting is held down, never killed, so there's no need to be hard on yourself when it comes back. See you tomorrow.

1130.title: Nataraja explained
1130.hook: the dancer's hair streams out sideways toward the ring of fire, and caught in it, with her hands folded, is a river
1130.howItsDone: In Nataraja bronzes the locks fly out toward the encircling ring of flames, with the small figure of Ganga and often a crescent moon among them; the story of Shiva catching the Ganga is told in the Ramayana and widely retold.

segments.voice: Yesterday in Nataraja explained, Apasmara: forgetting, held under the foot and never killed. Today, the hair and the fire around it.
screen: `REMEMBERING IS A STEP YOU KEEP TAKING.` · `TODAY: THE HAIR AND THE RING.`

segments.voice: Get close to a Nataraja bronze, closer than the guard would like, and look at the hair. It doesn't hang down. It flies out to both sides in long locks, like the spokes of a wheel, as if he's spinning so fast the hair can't keep up. The locks stretch toward the ring of flames that frames the figure. And tangled in them on one side is something tiny: a little woman, half of her shaped like flowing water, her hands folded. That's the river Ganga.
screen: `THE HAIR FLIES OUT LIKE SPOKES.` → `TOWARD THE RING OF FLAMES.` → `CAUGHT IN THE LOCKS: GANGA.`

segments.voice: Why is a river in his hair? The Ramayana tells it. A king named Bhagiratha practiced long austerities to bring the heavenly Ganga down to earth, so her water could reach the ashes of his ancestors. The gods agreed. But a river falling from heaven would crash into the earth and break it. Someone had to catch her. So Bhagiratha turned to Shiva, and Shiva stood beneath the falling river and took her on his head. She disappeared into his matted locks and wandered there, slowed and gentled, until he let her out in streams that could flow across the land. So the wildest part of the image, the hair whipping out in the dance, turns out to be holding something with care. Near her there's often a crescent moon too, carried the same way. The storm is also a cradle. Now the ring of fire. People read it more than one way. Some see the world itself, the whole turning cosmos the dance happens inside. Some see time, going round and round. What's clear is where the dancer is. Not outside the ring, watching. Inside it, filling it, the hair reaching out to touch its edges, and the river he caught in there with him. When something comes down hard, a piece of news, a tidal wave of a week, the image suggests you don't have to stop it, or let it shatter you. It can land in something that slows it down, and go on gentler than it came.
screen: `BHAGIRATHA BRINGS DOWN THE GANGA.` · `SHIVA CATCHES HER IN HIS HAIR.` · `THE STORM IS ALSO A CRADLE.` · `THE DANCE IS INSIDE THE RING.` · then, large: `CATCH WHAT FALLS, AND LET IT GO ON GENTLER.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind something that's come down on you hard lately, a worry, a piece of news, a heavy load, and picture it landing not on your shoulders but somewhere soft, like water falling into a tangle of hair and losing its force. Breathe in and let it land; breathe out and let a little of it flow on, gentler than it came. If you pray, you can offer it to Shiva, or to God.

1131.title: Nataraja explained
1131.hook: in the temple at Chidambaram, a priest draws back a curtain beside the dancer, and behind it there seems to be nothing at all
1131.howItsDone: At the Nataraja temple in Chidambaram, Tamil Nadu, the dancing Shiva is worshiped daily with lamps, bathing and song, and priests at times draw back a curtain to show the Chidambara rahasya, an empty space hung with golden bilva leaves.

segments.voice: Yesterday in Nataraja explained, the flying hair caught the river Ganga, and the dance filled its ring of fire. Today, the whole dancer, and his home.
screen: `CATCH WHAT FALLS, AND LET IT GO ON GENTLER.` · `TODAY: THE WHOLE DANCE.`

segments.voice: At Chidambaram, in Tamil Nadu, the dancing Shiva isn't in a museum case. He stands in a hall with a golden roof, dressed, garlanded, bathed and sung to, while a crowd presses forward and oil lamps are waved in the dark. Temple tradition says this is where he danced for two sages who longed to see it: Patanjali, shown with the body of a serpent, and Vyaghrapada, whose name means tiger-foot. And beside the dancer hangs a curtain. At certain moments a priest draws it back, and the people lean in.
screen: `A HALL WITH A GOLDEN ROOF.` → `THE DANCE FOR TWO SAGES.` → `A CURTAIN BESIDE THE DANCER.`

segments.voice: Behind the curtain there seems to be nothing: an empty space, hung with a garland of golden bilva leaves. It's called the Chidambara rahasya, the secret of Chidambaram. The dancer is there in form, with arms and hair and fire. And right beside him, the same lord, with no form at all. Space. Tradition links this temple with space itself, the open sky the dance happens in. Now put the whole image back together, because a Shaiva teaching does exactly that. It reads the dance as doing five things at once. The drum: creation. The raised hand that says do not fear: preservation, keeping what's made. The flame: dissolution. The planted foot on Apasmara: concealment, the veil of forgetting that hides what's true. And the lifted foot the elephant hand points to: grace, release. Make, keep, end, hide, free: five acts, one dancer, never stopping. You've now met each piece: the calm face, the drum, the flame, the pointing hand, the figure underfoot, the hair and the ring. Laid side by side, they make one sentence. Everything moves, and the center is still. One foot lifted, one planted. A form you can see, beside a space you can't. And the curtain matters too. The secret isn't locked away. It's shown, on purpose, to anyone standing in the crowd. The tradition doesn't ask anyone to choose between the dancer and the empty space. It keeps them side by side, behind one curtain.
screen: `THE SECRET: AN EMPTY SPACE.` · `FIVE ACTS: MAKE, KEEP, END, HIDE, FREE.` · `ONE FOOT LIFTED, ONE PLANTED.` · `THE FORM BESIDE THE FORMLESS.` · then, large: `EVERYTHING MOVES, AND THE CENTER IS STILL.`

segments.voice: First notice everything that's moving, the breath, the heartbeat, sounds coming and going, thoughts flickering at the edges like flames, and let all of it move. Then notice what isn't moving, the space it all happens in, the quiet behind the sounds, and rest there, holding the dance and the space together without choosing. If you pray, you can say Shiva's name, or the name of God you use, into that space.
Nataraja explained. The whole dancer: five acts in one dance, a calm face in the motion, and beside him at Chidambaram, an empty space that is the same lord without form.
Your line: Nataraja explained. Moving and steady at once, like a river, or your own breath. Until tomorrow.

1132.title: the Shiva Sahasranama (selections)
1132.hook: a hymn made of nothing but names, and the first selection: Sthanu, the steady post
1132.howItsDone: Devotees of Shiva recite his sahasranama at home or in temples, often on Mondays or at Maha Shivaratri; in a temple archana, a priest may offer a flower, leaf or grain of rice at each name.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Nataraja explained, whole: one foot lifted, one planted, moving and steady at once. Today, a hymn of names begins.

A contact in your phone is saved as Mom. Your cousin calls the same woman Auntie. Her boss uses her last name. Her oldest friend has a nickname nobody else is allowed to use. One person, and every name catches her from a different side. Hindu tradition does this with the divine, on purpose, and at length. Some hymns are nothing but names, one after another, like beads on a string. Today i'll open one of them, a few names at a time: the Shiva Sahasranama.
screen: `ONE PERSON, MANY NAMES.` → `A HYMN MADE OF NAMES.` → `THE SHIVA SAHASRANAMA.`

segments.voice: Sahasranama is the hymn's own name for itself: the thousand names. Tradition keeps more than one hymn of Shiva's names. Some readers know it from the Mahabharata, the great epic; others from the Puranas, including the Shiva Purana. This one starts in the Mahabharata, because the setting is lovely. Krishna wants a son. So he travels to the Himalayas, to the hermitage of a sage named Upamanyu, a devotee of Shiva. Upamanyu tells Krishna what Shiva has done for him, and then hands him a gift that costs nothing: the names. Near the start of the list come a few short words. Sthira, the firm one. Sthanu, the post. Prabhu, the lord. Bhima, the fearsome one. Stay with Sthanu. It's a plain word: a post, a pillar, a tree stump that doesn't move when the wind blows. An odd thing to call a god, and it sits right next to yesterday's dancer, who never stops moving. The names don't argue with each other. They stack. Shiva is the dancer, and Shiva is the post, and a devotee is allowed to hold both. That's how a sahasranama works. No one name is asked to say everything. Each one is a small door, and you go through the doors one at a time. In temple worship, a priest may offer a flower, a leaf or a few grains of rice at each name, so the hymn becomes a slow walk of offerings.
screen: `SAHASRANAMA: THE THOUSAND NAMES.` · `KRISHNA VISITS UPAMANYU.` · `STHANU: THE STEADY POST.` · `EACH NAME A SMALL DOOR.`

segments.voice: Sit and let your spine rise like a pillar, the shoulders dropping around it, and let thoughts blow past like wind; a post doesn't argue with weather. On each out-breath, feel how little needs to move. If you pray, you can say the name Sthanu softly on the out-breath; if not, the word steady works just as well.
The Shiva Sahasranama. A hymn of Shiva's names, said one at a time, each name a door. Today's name from it: Sthanu, the steady post.
Your line: the Shiva Sahasranama, in selections. Someone you love answers to more names than the one you use, and so does Shiva. Rest well.

1133.title: the Shiva Sahasranama (selections)
1133.hook: the fierce god's gentlest names: Shankara and Shambhu, the ones who make things well
1133.howItsDone: Devotees greet Shiva with names like Shambho and Shankara in songs, chants and everyday speech, and the Shri Rudram, with its line namah shivaya, is chanted in Shiva temples, especially during abhisheka, the bathing of the linga.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Shiva Sahasranama opened, and Sthanu, the steady post, stood beside the dancer. Today, two gentle names.

What do you call someone who frightens people and is still the one they run to? Shiva sits in cremation grounds, smeared with ash, a snake around his neck. Yesterday's list held Bhima, the fearsome one. And yet, painted on bus windshields and sung at temple doors, the names you'll hear are soft ones. Shambho. Shankara. Two names from the same hymn, and they don't sound frightening at all.
screen: `FEARSOME, AND STILL RUN TO.` → `SHAMBHO. SHANKARA.` → `THE GENTLE NAMES.`

segments.voice: Start with Shankara. Tradition explains the name as the one who makes well-being: sham is ease, welfare, peace, and kara is the one who makes it. Shambhu sits beside it, explained as the one from whom well-being comes. Say them slowly and they almost sound like comfort. The same names turn up in a Vedic hymn to Rudra, the Shri Rudram, still chanted in temples. It opens by bowing to Rudra's anger, and to his arrows. It doesn't pretend he's harmless. But deep into the hymn it turns, and bows to him as Shambhu, as Shankara, and as Shiva, the auspicious one, and then as the one more auspicious still. That's where the words namah shivaya are heard: bowing to Shiva, inside a hymn that began by facing his anger. So when the sahasranama gives a devotee Bhima and Shankara in the same breath, it isn't confused. It's keeping the old pattern: the fierce one and the kind one are the same one. Plenty of people know this from their own lives. The aunt with the sharp tongue who drove across town when you were sick. The coach who scared you and then believed in you. A name like Shankara doesn't erase the fierceness. It says what the fierceness is for. In the stories, Shiva's terrible side burns away what harms, and what's left is well-being. A devotee who says Shankara is naming the end of that story, not just the middle.
screen: `SHANKARA: THE MAKER OF WELL-BEING.` · `SHAMBHU: WELL-BEING COMES FROM HIM.` · `THE RUDRAM: FROM ANGER TO SHIVA.` · `FIERCE AND KIND, THE SAME ONE.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one fierce thing in yourself, a quick temper, a stubborn streak, a no you say fast, and without sanding it down, ask it quietly what it's protecting, and wait. On each out-breath, let the edge stay, and let it turn toward what it guards. If you pray, you can say Shankara or Shambho as you breathe out; if not, let the breath carry the question.
The Shiva Sahasranama. Today's names from it: Shankara, the one who makes well-being, and Shambhu, from whom well-being comes. Fierce and kind, the same one.
Your line: the Shiva Sahasranama, in selections. Fierce and kind, it turns out, are the same one. See you tomorrow.

1134.title: the Shiva Sahasranama (selections)
1134.hook: Pashupati, lord of every creature, and in Shaiva teaching the lord who loosens the rope
1134.howItsDone: Shiva is worshipped as Pashupati at the Pashupatinath temple on the Bagmati river in Kathmandu, and Shaiva Siddhanta teachers explain their path through pati, pashu and pasha: the lord, the soul and the bond.

segments.voice: Yesterday the Shiva Sahasranama gave its gentle names, Shankara and Shambhu: the fierce one who makes things well. Today, the lord of creatures.

Kathmandu, early morning, beside the Bagmati river. Monkeys run along the temple walls. Pigeons crowd the stone steps. Pilgrims queue with marigolds, and a little way down the bank, smoke rises from the cremation ghats. The temple is Pashupatinath, and the name over its door is one of Shiva's: Pashupati. The animals wandering the courtyard are a fitting welcome, because the name is about them, and then about everyone.
screen: `A TEMPLE ON THE BAGMATI.` → `MONKEYS, PIGEONS, PILGRIMS.` → `PASHUPATI.`

segments.voice: Pashupati joins two words. Pati is lord, or protector. Pashu is a creature, the kind of animal that's tied up in a yard: a cow, a goat. So at its simplest, Pashupati is the lord of animals, the herdsman god who looks after every living thing, wild and tame. The name sits in the sahasranama lists. But Shaiva teachers took it further. In schools such as Shaiva Siddhanta, three words carry the teaching. Pati, the lord, is Shiva. Pashu is every soul, you and me included, called a creature because it's tied. And pasha is the rope that ties it. Teachers name its strands: a root ignorance that makes the soul feel small, the pull of past actions, and the hold of the changing world. On this reading, Pashupati isn't only the lord who owns the herd. He's the one who loosens the rope. It's a humbling name and a hopeful one. Humbling, because it puts everyone in the yard with the goats. Hopeful, because a rope can be untied. Look back over this week: Nataraja, the dancer in the ring of fire, never still. Then Sthanu, the post that never moves. Then Shankara and Shambhu, the fierce one who makes things well. And today Pashupati, who sets the tied one free. The names don't line up into one tidy picture. They keep turning him, the way you turn a stone in your hand to see every side.
screen: `PASHU, PATI: CREATURE, LORD.` · `PATI, PASHU, PASHA: LORD, SOUL, ROPE.` · `THE ONE WHO LOOSENS THE ROPE.` · `THIS WEEK: DANCER, POST, MAKER OF GOOD.`

segments.voice: Ask quietly what's pulling at you today, a worry, a habit, a grudge, a screen you keep reaching for, and without fighting it, feel where it tugs: the chest, the belly, the hands. On each out-breath, let the rope go a little slack, the way you'd loosen a knot without cutting it. If you pray, you can say Pashupati and offer the knot to Shiva; if not, let the breath loosen it.
The Shiva Sahasranama. Today's name from it: Pashupati, lord of every creature, and in Shaiva teaching, the lord of the soul who loosens its rope.
Your line: the Shiva Sahasranama, in selections. Lord of every creature, and the one who loosens what ties them. A week, done.
